extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator / early-18th-century literate public interested in manners, morals, and current affairs
extracted.subtask_description: A short periodical essay (The Spectator, 1709) combining moral commentary on manners (impertinence, whisperers, laughers), reflections on duelling customs, and brief news items; aimed at instructing and amusing polite readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Toleration of different kinds of loquacity
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘‘Therefore if it be true, that we women are also given to greater fluency of words than is necessary, sure one that disturbs but a room or a family is more to be tolerated, than one who draws together parishes and counties…’’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speech should be judged by its scale and consequence: a person who merely disturbs a room or family is more tolerable than one whose noisy behaviour gathers broader disturbance (parishes or counties). The passage contrasts private trivial talk with public, disruptive roaring that lacks the 'relish' of human faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities required of a lady's whispering maid
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘‘A gentlewoman who has a very delicate ear, wants a maid who can whisper, and help her in the government of her family. If the said servant can clear-starch, lisp, and tread softly, she shall have suitable encouragement in her wages.’’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical list of desirable servant attributes for delicate households: ability to whisper/soft-step, skill in clear-starching (neat laundry), and a lisp (softened speech). Presented as concrete hiring criteria in a satirical domestic vignette.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs and behaviour of an impertinent man
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of pretenders to business: ‘‘he shall keep you half an hour with your hat off, entertaining you with his consideration of that affair you spoke of… then when he is public enough, he immediately runs into secrets, and falls a whispering… Your pretender to business is never in secret, but in public.’’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Behavioural markers for identifying impertinent or vain men: long-winded public displays of 'business', feigned secrecy (whispering), use of verbal breaks and affectations (e.g. 'but however, thus far'), and a craving for observation and notice rather than genuine industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of impertinent characters (types)
rubrics_metrics.description: Character sketches (Umbra, Flyblow, Will Shoestring) as exemplars of impertinence: e.g., Flyblow ‘‘feeds on the sore part… tells you the worst passage of his life’’; Will Shoestring is vain about appearances (combing wig, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comic character-types to diagnose social failings: note recurring traits (obsequiousness, gossip, vanity) and verbal tics (Flyblow's frequent 'but') as diagnostic criteria for undesirable social company. The examples show how to distinguish different species of impertinence and prescribe appropriate responses (treat impotent malice with force).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dueling acceptable only in service or self-defence
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘‘If it were in my power, every man that drew his sword, unless in the Service, or purely to defend his life, person, or goods, from violence… should ride the wooden horse…’’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative rule: drawing a sword (duelling) is only defensible when performed in military service or as genuine defence of life, person, or property; otherwise it merits civil or corporal punishment. The essay argues for strict limitation of the custom of duelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed punishments for unlawful duelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested sanctions: first offence ride the wooden horse in the Tilt Yard, second offence stand in the pillory, third be prisoner in Bedlam for life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satirical but prescriptive sequence of escalating public punishments intended to deter the habit of duelling when not legitimately necessary. The passage gives specific penalties to illustrate the author's desire to eradicate the practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules of fair conduct in single combat (historical practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounts of past duelling customs: ‘‘the principals put on their pumps, and stripped to their shirts… the weapons were always equal… the party which happened to have the first man disarmed or killed, should yield as vanquished.’’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical criteria for an ‘honourable’ duel: equality of weapons, principals fighting (seconds originally stood by), stripping to shirts to show no concealed arms, and conventions (yielding when the side first disarmed/killed). The essay recounts how those rules evolved and sometimes produced perverse incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and obligations of seconds in duels
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘‘They used seconds, who were to see that all was upon the square, and make a faithful report of the whole combat… but the swords of those days being pretty long… the seconds fought…’’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originally seconds were guarantors of fairness and witnesses; practice shifted when seconds took active roles (even fighting), illustrating how ritual safeguards can mutate into additional causes of violence. The account serves as both description and warning about changing customs.

rubrics_metrics.name: When pistols are used in lieu of swords
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘‘Why, Sir Mark, in the beginning of July, a man would have been censured for want of courage… suppose an active, adroit, strong man, had insulted an awkward, or a feeble… Then, sir, they fought with pistols.’’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for changing weaponry: pistols are adopted where skill or physical advantage would make sword-fighting unfair; the shift reflects attempts to equalize the contest but raises moral questions about honour and the certainty of deadly outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic/social standard at Oxford: bow to learning, not fortune
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘‘…superiority is there given in proportion to men's advancement in wisdom and learning;… you shall see an earl walk bareheaded to the son of the meanest artificer, in respect to seven years more worth and knowledge than the nobleman is possessed of.’’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prescriptive social ideal: at Oxford, rank is subordinated to learning—deference and honour are given according to merit (knowledge) rather than birth or fortune. The passage uses this as a model of civility and the proper ordering of honours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority of the Oxonian almanack / empirical signs over fashionable error
rubrics_metrics.description: Anecdote defending the Oxonian computation of term dates: the author asserts the Oxford almanack is right even when the town differs, and cites the Westminster dog and other consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for trusting institutional/empirical authority (university almanack, animals' instincts) over fashionable or interest-driven calendars; practical consequences (forfeited recognisances, legal actions) are used to argue for adherence to learned authority.
